analysis.investment_thesis: Aditya Vision trades at INR 523.5 against a calculated Graham Number of approximately INR 91 — a 474% premium to intrinsic value that no margin of safety exists to justify. With operating cash flow deeply negative (-41 Cr in FY25), FCF deteriorating to -78 Cr, and P/B at 10.53x, this is a growth story priced for perfection, not a value investment.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 36% and Net Profit CAGR of 44.1% over 3 years demonstrate real business momentum
ROCE of 29.95% indicates the underlying retail operations are capital-efficient on a reported basis
Interest coverage of ~5.5x (Operating Income 175 Cr / Finance Cost 32 Cr) clears my 3.5x minimum threshold
key_risks: P/E of 61.37 and P/B of 10.53 are 4x and 7x above my maximum acceptable thresholds — extreme speculative premium
Free cash flow has deteriorated sharply: +13 Cr (FY22) → -78 Cr (FY25); reported profits are not translating into cash
Total Debt surged from 282 Cr (FY22) to 480 Cr (FY25) while the business burns cash — growth is externally financed
red_flags: Graham Number ~INR 91 vs. market price INR 523.5 — investor is paying 5.7x intrinsic value
Operating cash flow negative in 2 of last 4 years and worsening (-6 Cr in FY24, -41 Cr in FY25) — profits are an accounting entry, not cash in hand
Financing cash flow consistently positive (FY23: +69, FY24: +68, FY25: +94 Cr) — company is a capital-consuming machine dependent on external funding
No evidence of dividend payments — shareholders receive no cash return while management expands aggressively
analysis.detailed_analysis:
By every quantitative measure I have established over a lifetime of security analysis, Aditya Vision fails comprehensively. The P/E of 61.37 stands at four times my ceiling of 15; the P/B of 10.53 is seven times my preferred ceiling of 1.5. The calculated Graham Number — the geometric mean of earnings power and asset value — is approximately INR 91 per share (√(22.5 × EPS ~8.2 × BVPS ~45.2)). At INR 523.5, the market is demanding that you pay a 474% premium over this intrinsic anchor, leaving no margin of safety whatsoever. Mr. Market is in a state of euphoria about Bihar's consumer electronics boom, and he is asking you to share his excitement at your own expense.

More troubling than the valuation is the cash flow picture. A retailer reporting growing net profits (INR 35 Cr → 106 Cr) while simultaneously posting operating cash outflows of -41 Cr and free cash outflows of -78 Cr in FY25 is expanding its working capital and inventory at a pace that consumes real cash. The financing arm is filling the gap — total debt has jumped 70% to 480 Cr. Debt-to-equity of 0.65 breaches my 0.5 threshold, and this ratio will worsen if OCF does not turn positive. This is a company growing its way into a liquidity problem, not a conservatively financed enterprise with a durable competitive position. The intelligent investor requires both a low price and a strong balance sheet — here, neither condition is remotely satisfied.
